slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: How human-shaped machines are stepping out of science fiction and into our factories, homes, and daily lives

slides.heading: Why Human-Shaped?
slides.body: Our world is built for human bodies — doors, stairs, tools, workbenches. A robot with two arms and two legs can navigate and use the same infrastructure we do, without redesigning entire environments around it.

slides.heading: Who's Building Them?
slides.body: Tesla (Optimus), Figure AI, Boston Dynamics (Atlas), Agility Robotics (Digit), and Apptronik are all racing to deploy humanoid robots at scale. China's BYD and Xiaomi have also entered the competition, making this a global technology race.

slides.heading: From Lab to Factory Floor
slides.body: BMW, Amazon, and Tesla are already piloting humanoid robots on assembly lines to handle repetitive or ergonomically difficult tasks. These robots work alongside human employees rather than replacing entire production lines overnight.

slides.heading: The AI Brain Inside
slides.body: Modern humanoid robots use large neural networks trained on video of human motion, combined with real-time sensor fusion. This lets them generalize to new tasks — like picking up an unfamiliar object — without being reprogrammed each time.

slides.heading: The Hardest Engineering Problems
slides.body: Bipedal balance, dexterous hand control, and energy efficiency remain brutal challenges. A human can carry groceries up stairs with ease; replicating that gracefully in a robot still requires cutting-edge actuator design and real-time AI inference.

slides.heading: How Much Do They Cost?
slides.body: Current prototypes cost $50,000–$250,000 per unit, but manufacturers are targeting sub-$30,000 at mass-production volumes. Tesla has projected Optimus could eventually cost less than a car — a price point that would open consumer markets.

slides.heading: Safety and Regulation
slides.body: Unlike industrial robots caged behind fences, humanoids share space with people, raising new safety questions. Regulators in the US, EU, and Japan are developing frameworks for cobot standards, liability rules, and required safety certifications before widespread deployment.

slides.heading: The Jobs Question
slides.body: Economists are split: some warn of large-scale displacement in warehousing, logistics, and manufacturing; others argue robots will fill labor shortages in aging societies. The net impact depends heavily on how quickly adoption scales and whether retraining programs keep pace.

slides.heading: A Robot in Every Workplace?
slides.body: Humanoid robots have moved from sci-fi to factory floors in less than a decade. As AI, materials science, and manufacturing converge, the question is no longer if they'll be everywhere — but how soon, and on whose terms.
